title: Why rejoin UNIDO? Reforms, projects and the case for membership
label: 15 September 2026 · UNIDO evidence session
summary: Witnesses from the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO) explain the internal reforms they’ve made since the UK withdrew, give concrete examples of projects delivered with donor money (including UK support), and argue that rejoining gives the UK a voice in how UNIDO is run and helps scale practical industrial, energy and digital projects by connecting governments, private companies and finance.

speakers.label: Manuel Mattiat
speakers.name: Manuel Mattiat
speakers.role: Director and Chief of Cabinet, Office of the Chief of Cabinet, UNIDO

speakers.label: Rana Ghoneim
speakers.name: Rana Ghoneim

chapters.title: Why we're here and what changed since the UK's withdrawal
chapters.takeaway: UNIDO says it has reformed its internal systems and increased on-the-ground delivery since the UK left, and that the UK’s return would buy influence as well as funds.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We're here to hear why the UK is rejoining UNIDO and what has changed since you left. Lord German will start.

turns.speaker: Lord German
turns.text: What did UNIDO fix after the UK withdrew? What answers did you put in place for the UK's concerns at the time?

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: Thank you. UNIDO is the UN agency that helps countries build industry, add value to goods and connect them to markets. After the UK's withdrawal, we carried out big internal reforms: two restructurings, cuts in management layers (by not replacing retirees), and improvements in finance, procurement and HR.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: Those reforms aimed to make us faster and more efficient. In four years we've tripled the money we raise and doubled delivery of technical projects. For the first time this year we expect about £400 million of delivery on the ground.

chapters.title: How UNIDO changed its ways of working
chapters.takeaway: They decentralised procurement, trimmed bureaucracy and opened up to private companies to speed up and scale projects.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: We decentralised buying (so field teams can buy locally), improved results reporting, and used partners more. We also reached out to the private sector so companies can bring technology and know-how into new markets.

turns.speaker: Lord Hannay of Chiswick
turns.text: The UN overall is cutting down. What role is UNIDO playing in the Secretary-General's UN-wide reform — called UN80 — to avoid duplication and shrink back-office costs?

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: UN80 asks who does what best. We're saying: we focus on technical industrial work (engineers, economists, policy), and we should sometimes use other UN agencies for back-office tasks like procurement or payroll rather than doing everything ourselves.

turns.speaker: Jason Slater
turns.text: A practical UN80 example: we teamed up with UNOOSA — the UN Office for Outer Space Affairs — on 'Space4Industry' to use satellite data and AI for industrial planning and climate early warnings. It shows agencies can combine strengths.

chapters.title: Concrete projects funded with UK and other money
chapters.takeaway: They gave examples: UK-backed work on steel/cement carbon accounting, innovation links with Brazil, A2D pilots like Namibia hydrogen and Kenya biogas, plus tech tools for farmers in Ghana.

turns.speaker: Lord Stevenson of Balmacara
turns.text: Can you give two or three concrete examples of what UK money has actually paid for on the ground?

turns.speaker: Rana Ghoneim
turns.text: Yes. One: we’re working with UK expertise and industry on carbon accounting for steel and cement — that means creating consistent ways to measure emissions in those sectors so countries can trade and attract green investment.

turns.speaker: Rana Ghoneim
turns.text: Two: linking the UK innovation ecosystem with Brazil to design industrial decarbonisation road maps and bring UK universities and companies into Brazilian projects.

turns.speaker: Rana Ghoneim
turns.text: Three: our A2D (Accelerate-to-Demonstrate) facility — a rapid funding window — helps early-stage, ground-breaking pilots. With UK support we’ve backed things like Namibia’s first hydrogen production plan and biogas projects in Kenya’s tea industry.

turns.speaker: Lord Boateng
turns.text: We need projects that help farmers and processing so local economies grow. Any practical examples of that?

turns.speaker: Jason Slater
turns.text: In Ghana — funded by Japan, not the UK — we deployed a simple phone-based tool that lets farmers scan and trace rice to find post-harvest losses. In six months losses fell from 20% to 13%. It shows tech plus local partners can make a quick difference.

chapters.title: Energy, industry and scaling — the practical challenge
chapters.takeaway: UNIDO says energy must tie to industry (anchor customers) so mini-grids and investments are sustainable, and scaling needs private finance plus concessional loans.

turns.speaker: Baroness Verma
turns.text: I travel in Africa and still see huge areas without power. Where are investments heading and how do you measure that your work reaches people on the ground?

turns.speaker: Rana Ghoneim
turns.text: Energy isn't just electricity: it's the basis for industry. We push 'industrial transformation investment plans' so energy projects have industrial customers — firms that create enough demand (anchor loads) to make mini-grids viable and attract private investors.

turns.speaker: Rana Ghoneim
turns.text: Scaling needs two things: preparing countries to absorb larger concessional loans and attracting private capital. We work on pipelines and bankable projects so bigger finance flows to least developed countries and islands.

turns.speaker: Baroness Verma
turns.text: The local-level point matters: small industries and agronomists can be key. Tech helps, but local crop and soil expertise must be in the mix.

chapters.title: How UNIDO complements bilateral aid and the case for membership
chapters.takeaway: UNIDO argues membership gives the UK governance oversight and influence; being a big donor without membership limits political input on policy and budgets.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We already channel a lot of UK aid through agencies and direct projects. What's UNIDO doing that we can't get by funding a UK-led project directly? Why rejoin?

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: Two big points. First, UNIDO opens doors in markets where bilaterals may not have reach: our offices, country teams and private-sector links help companies enter new places. Second, membership gives the UK a seat at the table: you can take part in the industrial development board and influence how money is spent and policy is made.

turns.speaker: Baroness Lawlor
turns.text: I'm worried membership just makes you a talking shop. If the UK can fund projects it trusts, wouldn't that be better value?

turns.speaker: Jason Slater
turns.text: Funding projects works, but membership helps with the next step: attracting investors to scale. Membership also improves co-ordination — for example, combining funding from Japan or EU with UK programmes so a pilot can expand to national scale.

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: Also, membership helps us involve UK technical experts in our research and standards work — think industrial policy, carbon standards — and it gives UK firms the UNIDO 'seal' when entering markets.

chapters.title: Sustainability of reforms and closing points
chapters.takeaway: They say reforms are being institutionalised through partnerships, leadership training and new financing mechanisms, and believe UK membership helps lock in those changes.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: One last worry: these reforms look tied to the director-general. What if leadership changes and things slide back?

turns.speaker: Manuel Mattiat
turns.text: The DG has pushed reforms hard, but we've institutionalised many changes: new decentralised processes, financial footing and partnerships. We also recruit and train leaders so the reform isn't just one person's legacy.

turns.speaker: Jason Slater
turns.text: We're also building new financing approaches — finance coalitions, working with private capital and possibly funds inside UNIDO — to make programs sustainable beyond one leader's term.

turns.speaker: Rana Ghoneim
turns.text: On energy we focus on preparing bankable pipelines and institutions so private finance follows. That institutional work — not single pilots — is what will help scaling stick.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. This has helped the committee understand both the practical projects and the governance reasons the UK is considering rejoining UNIDO. Safe journey home.

turns.speaker: Baroness Bonham-Carter of Yarnbury
turns.text: And please keep supporting Lavazza — it matters on the coffee supply-chain work!
